title: Build vs. Buy: A CFO-Friendly Framework for Sourcing POI Data
summary: New financial framework compares build versus buy strategies for sourcing point of interest data
detailed: The article provides a three-year financial framework for companies deciding whether to build or buy Point of Interest (POI) data.
Coresight Research tracked thousands of US store openings and closures, illustrating the constant decay and refresh cycle required for location datasets.
Building in-house from open sources like the Overture Maps Foundation introduces hidden costs such as archiving, deduplication, categorization, and closure detection.
This framework matters to CFOs and product leaders evaluating the true headcount and infrastructure costs of maintaining proprietary location databases.
sentences: Somewhere in your company, a product manager or data lead has probably said it already: “We could just build our own places database.” Maybe they’re right.
Point of interest (POI) data, the records of where stores, clinics, restaurants and other businesses are, sits underneath site selection models, delivery apps, risk scoring and ad targeting.
Getting it wrong is expensive.
This piece is for the person who has to sign off on that choice.
You’ll get a way to price both paths over three years, the cost lines that usually get left off the slide, and a short list of situations where building is honestly the better call.
The first thing to understand about places data is that it decays.
Stores open, close, relocate, rebrand and change their hours, and every one of those events is a record somebody has to fix.
Coresight Research gives a sense of the volume.
By the middle of 2026 it had tracked 3,321 US store closures and 3,215 openings, according to Retail TouchPoints’ September coverage.
And that was a quiet half-year.
Closures were down 44% from the same point in 2025, and openings were at their lowest midyear level since 2020.
So even in a slow year, you get roughly 6,500 announced changes in six months, and those are only the chains big enough to be tracked.
The count leaves out the independent café that shut without notice, the dentist who moved two blocks over, and the gym that turned into a pickleball club.
Those are exactly the records that make a dataset feel stale to the people using it.
For a CFO, this changes the shape of the question.
You aren’t buying an asset once.
You’re signing up for a refresh cycle whether you build or buy, and what you’re really deciding is who runs that cycle and what each round costs.
Building used to mean scraping the web from scratch.
Today most teams start from open data, and the best-known option is the Overture Maps Foundation, which publishes a free Places dataset with each monthly release.
Its January 2026 release held about 72.4 million place records, according to an analysis by data consultant Mark Litwintschik.
That’s a serious head start, and it keeps improving.
Overture’s August 2026 release notes report that one contributor’s US data grew by 1.46 million places, and that 1.64 million more places now carry an “open” operating status.
A free starting file still isn’t a finished database, though.

Here’s what your team would own:
Archiving: Overture removes old releases after 60 days.
If you need to reproduce last quarter’s model, you need your own copies.
Deduplication and matching: Two sources describing the same coffee shop with slightly different addresses have to become one record.
Categorization: Overture replaced its old categories field with a new taxonomy during 2026.
Every upstream schema change becomes a migration on your side.
Closure detection: Knowing a place closed is much harder than knowing it opened, because closed businesses rarely announce anything.
Licensing review: Open licenses differ, and your legal team will want to know what you can show or resell in a customer-facing product.
It’s just work that never ends, and work that never ends is headcount.
When a build proposal lands on your desk, the infrastructure estimate is usually there.
These five are the ones that tend to be missing.
How many people keep this current after launch, at fully loaded cost?
What does one monthly or quarterly update cost in compute and review time?
Can we walk away, and what can we keep doing with the data if we do?
That last row points at buying, on purpose.
Vendor contracts deserve the same skepticism as internal plans.
Usage restrictions, redistribution limits and renewal increases are real costs, and they tend to surface in year three.
You’ve probably seen Gartner’s estimate that poor data quality costs organizations an average of $12.9 million a year.
Before that figure goes into a board deck, it helps to know where it came from.
It traces back to a 2020 Gartner survey of reference customers of data quality vendors, who estimated their own costs, as this breakdown of the number explains.
It isn’t a representative sample, and it says nothing specific about location data.
A more useful exercise is pricing your own failure modes.
If a delivery app sends a driver to a restaurant that closed in June, what does the refund plus the annoyed customer cost?
If a site selection model counts three competitors that shut last spring, what’s a bad ten-year lease worth?
Those are the numbers that belong in your model.
The entries are placeholders to show the mechanics.
Swap in your own salary bands and vendor quotes.

Pipeline, matching logic, storage: about 2 engineers for 6 months
Count maintenance at full loaded cost, every single year: Planning has a way of stopping at launch day.
Over three years, the people keeping the data current usually cost more than the people who built the pipeline.
Put a dollar value on delay: If the business case depends on POI data and building adds six months, that’s six months of benefit you never collect.
Then total each column across three years.
If the build column still comes out lower and the risks in the bottom row feel manageable, building might be the right answer.
That happens more often than vendors like to admit.
There are situations where building wins, and a framework that pretends otherwise isn’t worth much.
The data is your product: If you sell maps or location intelligence, owning the pipeline is your moat.
Nobody covers your niche: Maybe you need EV chargers with connector types, or informal markets in a region commercial providers barely touch.
You need redistribution rights that no license will grant at a sensible price.
You already have people in the field: A company whose reps or inspectors visit locations every week has a verification network most data teams would envy.
